variants.name: Vapor middleware / responder chain
variants.idiom_name: AsyncMiddleware.respond(to:chainingTo: next: AsyncResponder) async throws -> Response
variants.implementation_notes: Vapor ships the chain: a type conforming to `Middleware` or `AsyncMiddleware` implements `respond(to:chainingTo:)`, receives the next `Responder` and either calls `try await next.respond(to: request)` or short-circuits by throwing an `Abort`; `app.middleware.use(_:)` appends a link, `app.grouped(_:)` scopes links to routes, and the route closure is the terminal handler. Requests traverse the list in registration order and responses in reverse, and ready-made links such as `CORSMiddleware`, `FileMiddleware` and `ErrorMiddleware` cover the usual pipeline.
pitfalls: CORSMiddleware must be registered with at: .beginning and before ErrorMiddleware, otherwise error responses leave the server without CORS headers.
Throwing bypasses the response handling of later middleware, so an error middleware must be registered first to observe it.
Middleware are shared across event loops; per-request state belongs on the Request, not on the middleware value.

variants.name: Protocol-based handler with ordered successors
variants.idiom_name: protocol Handler { func handle(_ request: Request) -> Response? } plus an ordered [any Handler]
variants.implementation_notes: Outside Vapor, Swift protocols give the classic structure without inheritance: a `Handler` protocol, concrete conforming types, and either a successor property or - much more common in Swift - an ordered array of `any Handler` walked until one returns a non-nil result. Structs are the default so handler state is copied rather than shared; classes are needed only when identity matters. The terminal outcome must be explicit because the language offers no unhandled-request signal.
pitfalls: Existential `any Handler` boxes each element and adds a dynamic call per hop; keep the array short or use generics for a fixed chain.
A class handler that stores its successor while the successor stores the previous link creates a retain cycle.
Mutating the handler array while a dispatch is in flight is a data race under strict concurrency checking; make the chain immutable.
